prompt: Give a code example in C++ that illustrates C++20 modules.
completion:
Below is a *minimal, “real‑world”* C++20 modules example that compiles with **Clang 18+** or **GCC 13+** (the latter only supports the *draft* TS).  
It shows:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `math.mod.cpp` | **module interface** (the public API) |
| `math.impl.cpp` | **module implementation** (private helpers) |
| `main.cpp` | A normal translation unit that **imports** the `math` module |
| `module.map` | Optional “module map” to help older toolchains locate the module source (GCC, older Clang). |

> **Tip** – If you use a recent enough compiler, you can skip `module.map` and just compile the two module files as separate modules; the compiler will pick them up automatically.

---

## 1.  The Module Interface (`math.mod.cpp`)

```cpp
// math.mod.cpp  ── module interface file
export module math;          // <-- module name

// Public interface ---------------------------------------------------------
export inline int add(int a, int b) noexcept {
    return a + b;
}

export inline int multiply(int a, int b) noexcept {
    return a * b;
}
```

- `export module math;` declares the *module name* (`math`).
- `export` before a declaration exposes it to code that `import`s the module.
- Because this is an **interface** file, all symbols you want public must be `export`‑ed.

---

## 2.  The Module Implementation (`math.impl.cpp`)

```cpp
// math.impl.cpp  ── module implementation file
module math;                 // <-- same module name

// Private helper (not exported, only visible inside this module)
int square(int x) noexcept { return x * x; }

// A non‑exported helper that the exported function can use
int internal_add(int a, int b) noexcept {
    return add(a, b);        // calls the exported `add`
}
```

- `module math;` (no `export`) opens the *same* module for implementation work.
- Anything not marked `export` stays hidden from the outside world.

---

## 3.  The Client (`main.cpp`)

```cpp
// main.cpp  ── client translation unit
import <iostream>;           // standard library headers (implicit modules)
import math;                  // import the math module

int main() {
    int x = 7, y = 3;
    std::cout << "add(" << x << ", " << y << ") = "
              << add(x, y) << '\n';

    std::cout << "multiply(" << x << ", " << y << ") = "
              << multiply(x, y) << '\n';

    return 0;
}
```

- `import math;` brings *only* the exported names (`add`, `multiply`) into scope.
- Standard headers are still included via `<...>` (they are provided by the compiler as *built‑in modules*).

---

## 4.  Optional Module Map (`module.map`)

GCC and some older Clang builds cannot find the module source files automatically.  
The module map tells the compiler where to look:

```text
# module.map  ── for GCC and older Clang
module math { interface "math.mod.cpp"; implementation "math.impl.cpp"; }
```

Place this file in the same directory as the source files.

---

## 5.  Build Instructions

> **Clang (recommended)**  
> ```bash
> # Compile the module (both interface & implementation)
> clang++ -std=c++20 -fmodules -c math.mod.cpp -o math.mod.o
> clang++ -std=c++20 -fmodules -c math.impl.cpp -o math.impl.o
> 
> # Compile the client
> clang++ -std=c++20 main.cpp math.mod.o math.impl.o -o app
> 
> ./app
> # Output:
> # add(7, 3) = 10
> # multiply(7, 3) = 21
> ```

> **GCC (experimental)**  
> ```bash
> # Compile module interface & implementation
> g++ -std=c++20 -fmodules-ts -c math.mod.cpp -o math.mod.o
> g++ -std=c++20 -fmodules-ts -c math.impl.cpp -o math.impl.o
> 
> # Compile the client (note: GCC needs the module map)
> g++ -std=c++20 -fmodules-ts -fmodule-map=module.map main.cpp math.mod.o math.impl.o -o app
> 
> ./app
> # Same output
> ```

> **Visual Studio**  
> Visual Studio 2022 (17.8+) supports C++20 modules.  
> Create a *Module Interface* file `math.mod.cpp`, add it to the project, and import it in `main.cpp`. Build as usual.

---

## 6.  What You Learned

| Feature | How it Appears |
|---------|----------------|
| **Module declaration** | `module math;` |
| **Exported symbols** | `export inline int add(...)` |
| **Implementation-only code** | `module math;` (no `export`) |
| **Importing a module** | `import math;` |
| **Compiling modules** | Separate compile commands (`-c`) + link step |

Modules give you a *clean, language‑level* way to organize code, replace header files, and get better compile‑time guarantees. Happy modular coding!
